course_title: Young Men Against Gender Based Violence
course_description: This course is designed for young Nigerian men to explore positive masculinity and prevent gender-based violence.

modules.title: Understanding Gender & Masculinity
modules.opening_story:
Meet Emeka.

Emeka is 24, from Onitsha. He grew up hearing the same things every Nigerian boy hears:

"Real men don't cry." "You are the man — you must provide." "Control your woman or she will disrespect you."

His father said it. His uncles said it. His church said it. His friends still say it.

But lately, Emeka has been thinking. His younger sister was beaten by her boyfriend. When Emeka told his uncle, the uncle said — "Maybe she provoked him. A man has to show authority."

Emeka felt something wrong with that answer. But he didn't have the words to explain why.

Today, we give him — and you — those words.

lessons.title: Sex vs Gender
lessons.content:
These two words are often used as if they mean the same thing. They do not.

SEX is biological — the body you were born with. Male or female. Determined by chromosomes, hormones, and anatomy.

GENDER is social — the rules, roles, and expectations that society places on people because of their sex.

One comes from nature. The other was built by people.

lessons.title: The Key Insight
lessons.content:
Here is the most important thing we will say in this entire course:

You were born male. But everything you learned about "how to be a man" — that was taught to you.

By your father. Your uncles. Your school. Your religion. Your community. Your peers.

Some of those lessons were good and worth keeping. Some were harmful — and can be changed.

lessons.title: What is Positive Masculinity?
lessons.content:
Masculinity is the way men express themselves in the world. But there is not just one way to be a man.

Harmful masculinity says: dominate, control, never feel.

Positive masculinity says: lead with respect, feel without shame, protect without controlling, be strong AND kind.

One traps you. The other sets you free. This course is about choosing freedom.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: What is the main difference between sex and gender?
options: A) They mean the same thing
B) Sex is biological; gender is built by society
C) Gender is biological; sex is built by society
D) Both are built by society
quiz.feedback: Correct! Sex = what you are born with. Gender = what society teaches you to be. This is the foundation of everything in this course.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: Which of these is a harmful gender norm?
options: A) Men should be kind to their children
B) Men must never show weakness or cry
C) Men should listen and respect women
D) Men can ask for help when they need it
quiz.feedback: Correct! Telling men never to show emotion cuts them off from their humanity — and harms those around them.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: Positive masculinity means a man should be:
options: A) Soft, weak, and passive
B) Unable to lead or make decisions
C) Strong, kind, respectful and emotionally honest
D) The same as a woman
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. Positive masculinity is about being a fuller, freer, better man — one who leads with respect, not fear.

modules.title: Harmful Norms & Toxic Masculinity
modules.opening_story:
Meet Chidi.

Chidi is 19. When his best friend Tolu started crying after losing his job, Chidi felt deeply uncomfortable. He told Tolu: "Oga, men don't cry. Pull yourself together."

Three weeks later, Tolu stopped answering his phone. His family found him in his room. He had taken his own life.

Chidi has not forgiven himself since. He keeps asking: "What if I had let him cry? What if I had just listened?"

Today, we explore the norms that told Chidi — and all of us — that men cannot feel. And what those norms cost us.

lessons.title: What Are Harmful Gender Norms?
lessons.content:
Harmful gender norms are beliefs about men that sound like truth but are actually damaging.

They include: "A man must never show weakness." "Men are naturally aggressive — it's in their nature." "A real man controls his household." "If a woman disrespects you, you have the right to correct her."

These are not facts. They are teachings. And they cause real damage — to women, children, and men themselves.

lessons.title: What is Toxic Masculinity?
lessons.content:
Toxic masculinity is not an insult to men. It is the name for a specific set of harmful ideas about manhood.

It describes behaviours and beliefs like: using violence to show strength, suppressing all emotion except anger, believing women must be controlled, seeing asking for help as weakness, and using sexual conquest to prove manhood.

Toxic masculinity hurts the men who practice it — with mental illness, isolation, and broken relationships — and it hurts everyone around them.

lessons.title: The Cost of Toxic Norms
lessons.content:
In Nigeria, men die younger than women. Men are less likely to see a doctor. Men are more likely to take their own lives in silence.

This is not because men are weaker. It is because they are taught that seeking help is shameful.

The same norms that harm women are slowly destroying men from the inside.

Changing these norms is not about making men weak. It is about keeping men alive, healthy, and connected to the people they love.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: Toxic masculinity is best described as:
options: A) An insult that attacks all men
B) A set of harmful beliefs about what manhood requires
C) A medical condition affecting some men
D) Normal male behaviour
quiz.feedback: Correct. Toxic masculinity is not about all men — it is about specific harmful ideas that hurt men and those around them.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: Which of these is a sign of toxic masculinity?
options: A) A man cries when his parent dies
B) A man asks his friend for advice
C) A man uses violence to settle arguments
D) A man cooks for his family
quiz.feedback: Correct. Using violence to resolve conflict is a key expression of toxic masculinity — and it is learned, not natural.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: Why do men in Nigeria have shorter life expectancy on average?
options: A) Men are biologically weaker
B) Men are taught that seeking help is shameful
C) Men work harder than women
D) Men eat less healthy food
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. The norms that stop men from seeking help are literally costing them years of their lives.

modules.title: Introduction to SGBV
modules.opening_story:
Meet Musa.

Musa is 26, from Kaduna. One evening, his neighbour Fatima knocked on his door with a swollen face and trembling hands. She said her husband had beaten her again.

Musa felt something rise in his chest. But then he heard his father's voice: "Don't enter another man's marriage. It's not your business."

So Musa said: "Sorry, aunty. Go and settle it between yourselves."

Fatima went home. Two months later, she was admitted to hospital.

Today, Musa is a man who wishes he had known better. This module gives you the knowledge Musa needed.

lessons.title: What is SGBV?
lessons.content:
SGBV stands for Sexual and Gender-Based Violence. It refers to any harmful act committed against a person's will, based on their gender or sex.

SGBV is not just physical beating. It includes: Physical violence (hitting, kicking, pushing). Sexual violence (rape, assault, harassment, unwanted touching). Emotional/psychological violence (threats, humiliation, control, isolation). Economic violence (controlling money, stopping someone from working). Harmful traditional practices (child marriage, FGM).

SGBV happens in homes, schools, workplaces, churches, mosques, and communities. It crosses every religion, tribe, and class.

lessons.title: Who Are the Victims?
lessons.content:
SGBV affects mostly women and girls — but not exclusively.

In Nigeria: 1 in 3 women have experienced physical violence. 1 in 4 girls are married before age 18. Boys and men can also be victims — especially of sexual violence and emotional abuse.

SGBV is not caused by what someone wears, where they go, or how they behave. It is caused by the person who chooses to commit violence. Victims are never to blame.

lessons.title: The Impact of SGBV
lessons.content:
SGBV does not just hurt the person it happens to. It damages entire communities.

Effects on survivors: Physical injuries (sometimes permanent). Mental health damage — depression, PTSD, anxiety, suicidal thoughts. Economic loss — inability to work or study. Social isolation — shame, stigma, silence.

Effects on communities: Broken families. Lower school enrollment for girls. Reduced productivity and economic growth. Cycles of violence passing from generation to generation.

Silence protects violence. Knowledge breaks that silence.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: SGBV includes which of the following?
options: A) Only physical beating
B) Only rape
C) Physical, sexual, emotional, economic violence and harmful practices
D) Only violence between strangers
quiz.feedback: Correct. SGBV is far broader than most people realise — it includes emotional, economic, and traditional forms of harm, not just physical violence.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: Who is responsible for SGBV?
options: A) The victim, for their behaviour or dress
B) The person who commits the violence
C) Both equally
D) Society, not individuals
quiz.feedback: Correct. The responsibility lies entirely with the person who chooses to commit violence. Victims are never to blame — ever.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: SGBV affects communities by:
options: A) Reducing girls' school enrollment
B) Causing cycles of violence across generations
C) Breaking families and reducing economic growth
D) All of the above
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. SGBV is not a private matter — its effects ripple through families, schools, economies, and generations.

modules.title: Root Causes of SGBV
modules.opening_story:
Meet the Okafor household.

Mr. Okafor earns all the money. Mrs. Okafor stays home with the children. When she asks for money to buy food, he says: "Whose money is it? You will use it as I say."

Their son, Junior, watches everything. He is 8 years old.

By the time Junior is 25, he believes that a man's money gives him the right to control a woman's body, movement, and voice.

Junior never hit anyone. But he controls his girlfriend's phone. He decides where she can go. He monitors her friends.

Junior learned this. Not from evil — but from what he watched every day growing up.

Today we trace the roots.

lessons.title: Power Imbalance
lessons.content:
The single biggest root cause of SGBV is unequal power — when one person believes they have the right to control, own, or dominate another.

Power imbalances show up as: Economic power ("I earn the money, so I decide everything"). Physical power (using size or strength to intimidate). Social power (using status or title to silence others). Institutional power (when laws and systems protect abusers, not survivors).

Where there is unchecked power, abuse follows. Not always. But far too often.

lessons.title: Culture and Socialisation
lessons.content:
Culture shapes what we believe is normal. Socialisation is how those beliefs are passed on — through family, religion, media, peers, and community.

In many Nigerian communities, culture teaches: that men are naturally dominant; that women must be submissive and silent; that family matters must stay private; that a man's authority is sacred.

These teachings are not facts. They are traditions. And traditions can be examined, challenged, and changed.

Culture is powerful. But it is also made by people — and can be remade by people.

lessons.title: Economic Factors
lessons.content:
Poverty and economic inequality create conditions where SGBV can thrive.

When a woman has no income, no savings, and no access to resources, she may feel trapped in an abusive relationship with no way out.

When a man faces unemployment and financial failure, and his identity is built entirely on "being the provider," the shame can turn into aggression.

Economic exclusion of women from education and financial independence is a structural driver of gender-based violence. Ending SGBV means also fighting for economic justice.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: What is the single biggest root cause of SGBV?
options: A) Men's natural aggression
B) Women's provocative behaviour
C) Unequal power between people
D) Poverty alone
quiz.feedback: Correct. SGBV is rooted in power imbalance — the belief that one person has the right to control another. This is learned, not natural.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: Socialisation means:
options: A) Going out with friends
B) How beliefs are passed on through family, religion, media and community
C) Learning in school only
D) A government programme
quiz.feedback: Correct. Socialisation is how norms and beliefs are transmitted across generations — and how harmful gender norms are kept alive.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: How does economic inequality contribute to SGBV?
options: A) Poor men are naturally more violent
B) Women with no income may feel trapped in abusive situations
C) Economic issues have nothing to do with SGBV
D) Wealth prevents all forms of abuse
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. Economic dependency can trap survivors in abusive situations — which is why women's financial independence is key to ending SGBV.

modules.title: Role of Men as Change Agents
modules.opening_story:
Meet Tunde.

Tunde is 30. He works in a Lagos office. One afternoon, a colleague makes a degrading joke about a female colleague — the whole room laughs.

Tunde wants to speak. His heart is beating fast. But a voice in his head says: "Don't make it awkward. It's just a joke. Nobody will thank you."

He stays silent. But the woman he defended in his mind goes home that day feeling invisible.

Later that week, Tunde's younger sister tells him she is experiencing harassment at her job. She says no one speaks up for her.

Tunde sits quietly. And he realises: he was the type of person his sister was hoping for — and he chose silence.

This module is about choosing differently.

lessons.title: Why Men Must Be Part of the Solution
lessons.content:
For too long, gender-based violence has been framed as "a women's issue." This is wrong — and dangerous.

Men commit the vast majority of GBV. Men hold most social, economic, and political power. And men have enormous influence over other men.

This means men are not just part of the problem. Men are essential to the solution.

When a man speaks up, other men listen in ways they don't when women speak. That influence is powerful — and carries responsibility.

lessons.title: What Allyship Looks Like
lessons.content:
Being an ally means actively using your position and voice to support those who are being harmed. Allyship is not just "not being abusive." It is taking action.

Practical allyship: Speaking up when you hear a sexist joke. Refusing to laugh at content that mocks women. Supporting a friend you think is being abused. Calling out a friend when his behaviour is controlling. Modelling respectful relationships in your own life.

Allyship is not a performance. It is a daily practice.

lessons.title: Personal Responsibility
lessons.content:
Change starts with you. Not with the government. Not with a campaign. With the choices you make every single day.

Your personal responsibility includes: Examining your own behaviours and attitudes honestly. Recognising how you may have benefited from gender inequality. Making a commitment — not just to avoid harm, but to actively prevent it. Holding yourself accountable when you fall short.

Nobody is perfect. But everyone can improve. And every improvement matters.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: Why is male involvement essential in ending GBV?
options: A) Women cannot solve this problem alone
B) Men hold significant social influence and power, and mostly commit GBV
C) Only men can make laws
D) Women don't understand the issue
quiz.feedback: Correct. Men's social influence — especially over other men — is one of the most powerful tools for changing norms and ending GBV.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: Allyship means:
options: A) Not committing violence yourself
B) Actively using your voice and position to support those being harmed
C) Signing a petition
D) Agreeing with women on everything
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. Allyship is active, not passive. It means taking visible action — speaking up, calling out, and modelling respectful behaviour.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: Personal responsibility in ending GBV starts with:
options: A) Waiting for government to act
B) Blaming other men
C) Honestly examining your own behaviours and attitudes
D) Educating only women
quiz.feedback: Correct. Change begins with self-examination. Before you can change others, you must be honest about your own choices and their impact.

modules.title: Healthy Masculinity & Relationships
modules.opening_story:
Meet Emeka again.

Emeka has been learning. He is now in a relationship with Adaeze, a woman he deeply respects.

But he is confused about some things. When he is stressed, he shuts down and goes silent. Adaeze says he makes her feel invisible.

One evening, they have a disagreement. Emeka raises his voice. Adaeze flinches.

He sees her flinch. And for the first time, he really sees it.

He sits down. He breathes. And he says: "I'm sorry. Can we start again?"

That moment changes everything. Today, we talk about what healthy relationships actually look like — and the skills that build them.

lessons.title: Consent — The Foundation of Everything
lessons.content:
Consent means freely, enthusiastically, and clearly agreeing to something.

Consent must be: Freely given (not under pressure or fear). Reversible (a person can change their mind at any time). Informed (both people understand what they're agreeing to). Enthusiastic (an uncertain "yes" is not a full yes). Specific (saying yes to one thing does not mean yes to everything).

Consent applies to sex. But also to everyday decisions in relationships — where you go, who you see, what you share.

A relationship without consent is not a relationship. It is control.

lessons.title: Communication and Conflict
lessons.content:
Healthy relationships require honest, respectful communication — especially during conflict.

Signs of healthy communication: Listening to understand, not just to respond. Expressing feelings without blame ("I feel..." not "You always..."). Taking responsibility for your own emotions. Being willing to take a break when conversations get too heated. Returning to difficult conversations when both people are calm.

Signs of unhealthy communication: Shouting, threatening, or using silence as punishment. Bringing up old arguments to win the current one. Refusing to listen or dismissing your partner's feelings.

lessons.title: Emotional Intelligence
lessons.content:
Emotional intelligence (EQ) is the ability to understand, express, and manage your own emotions — and to recognise the emotions of others.

Men are often taught to suppress emotions. This creates emotional illiteracy — the inability to name, process, or communicate feelings. And it damages relationships.

Building your EQ: Naming your emotions accurately. Pausing before reacting in anger. Recognising when someone you love is struggling. Being able to apologise genuinely. Asking for help when you need it.

Emotional intelligence is not weakness. It is the foundation of every strong relationship and every great leader.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: Which of the following is TRUE about consent?
options: A) Once someone says yes, they cannot change their mind
B) Silence means yes
C) Consent must be freely given, enthusiastic and reversible
D) Consent only applies to sex
quiz.feedback: Correct. Consent can be withdrawn at any time. It must be enthusiastic — not just the absence of a 'no'. And it applies to all areas of a relationship.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: Emotional intelligence means:
options: A) Being overly emotional or sensitive
B) Understanding and managing your own emotions and recognising others'
C) Hiding your feelings to stay strong
D) Only women need emotional skills
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. EQ is not about being emotional — it's about understanding emotions and using that to communicate and connect well.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: Which is a sign of unhealthy communication in a relationship?
options: A) Taking a break when a conversation gets too heated
B) Saying 'I feel hurt' instead of 'you hurt me'
C) Using silence as punishment
D) Listening carefully before responding
quiz.feedback: Correct. Using silence as punishment is emotional control — a manipulation tactic, not a healthy conflict resolution strategy.

modules.title: Bystander Intervention
modules.opening_story:
Meet Bello.

Bello is 22, from Kano. He is walking home with his friend Danladi when Danladi grabs his girlfriend's wrist — hard — and says: "You will not embarrass me in front of my friend."

The girlfriend winces. She goes silent. She looks at the ground.

Bello sees everything. His heart pounds. He thinks: "This is not my business. They will settle it."

But then he looks at her face. He has seen that face before — on his mother, years ago.

Bello stops walking. He clears his throat. And he says: "Danladi, bros — let's go get some water. Leave her small."

It was a small moment. But it changed everything for that woman — and for Bello.

Today, we learn how to be Bello.

lessons.title: Recognising Abuse
lessons.content:
Abuse is not always obvious. It does not always look like a black eye or a hospital visit.

Warning signs of abuse in relationships: A partner is controlled — their phone, money, movements, friendships. They are frequently belittled or humiliated in public. They seem afraid of their partner's reactions. They make excuses for their partner's behaviour. They are isolated from family and friends.

You do not need to be certain to be concerned. If something feels wrong, it usually is.

lessons.title: How to Intervene Safely — The 5Ds
lessons.content:
Intervening does not mean becoming a hero or risking violence. It means doing something — however small — that disrupts the abuse.

The 5Ds of Bystander Intervention: Direct — speak up calmly: "Hey, that's not okay." Distract — interrupt the situation: "Bello! Come, let's go." Delegate — get someone else involved if you can't act safely. Delay — check in with the person after: "Are you okay?" Document — record safely if it is safe to do so.

Safety first — always. If direct intervention feels dangerous, use distraction or delegation instead.

lessons.title: Supporting Survivors
lessons.content:
If someone tells you they are being abused, your response in that moment matters enormously.

What to do: Believe them. Listen without judgment. Tell them it is not their fault. Ask what they need: "How can I support you?" Share resources — helplines, shelters, legal support. Respect their choices — do not force them to leave if they are not ready. Check in with them regularly.

What NOT to do: Ask "What did you do to provoke it?" Advise them to "just leave" without a plan. Tell other people their story without permission. Minimise what happened.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: Which is a warning sign that someone may be experiencing abuse?
options: A) They have a busy social life
B) They seem afraid of their partner's reactions
C) They argue sometimes with their partner
D) They earn less than their partner
quiz.feedback: Correct. Fear of a partner's reactions — walking on eggshells, flinching, excessive appeasement — is one of the clearest warning signs of an abusive relationship.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: If you cannot safely intervene directly, you should:
options: A) Do nothing — it is not your business
B) Shout at the abuser
C) Distract or delegate — find a safe way to disrupt the situation
D) Record and post on social media immediately
quiz.feedback: Correct. The 5Ds give you options. Choose the one that is safest in the moment.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: When supporting a survivor, you should:
options: A) Ask what they did to provoke the situation
B) Force them to leave the relationship immediately
C) Believe them, listen without judgment, and ask what they need
D) Tell their family so others can help decide for them
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. Believing and listening without judgment are the most powerful things you can offer a survivor. Their choices must remain theirs.

modules.title: Peer Influence & Leadership
modules.opening_story:
Meet Chukwudi.

Chukwudi is 21. He is the most respected person in his friend group. When he speaks, everyone listens.

One night, the boys are drinking and one of them starts talking about a girl in degrading terms. Everyone laughs. The conversation escalates.

Chukwudi laughs too — at first.

But then he thinks of his 16-year-old sister. And he imagines someone talking about her this way.

He stops laughing. He says: "Abeg, that's somebody's sister. Let's change the topic."

There is a moment of silence. And then someone else says: "You're right. My bad." The conversation shifts.

Chukwudi didn't give a speech. He didn't shout. He just used the influence he already had — and it worked.

lessons.title: Understanding Your Influence
lessons.content:
Every man has influence — over his friends, his siblings, his colleagues, his community.

Influence is not reserved for pastors, politicians, or people with large followings. Influence is in everyday moments: The joke you laugh at or refuse to laugh at. The comment you make or stay silent about. The story you share on social media. The way you treat women in front of other men.

You are already shaping the men around you. The question is: what are you shaping them into?

lessons.title: Leading by Example
lessons.content:
The most powerful form of leadership is not what you say — it is what you do consistently.

You become a role model when: You speak respectfully about and to women — always. You call out harmful jokes, even at the cost of short-term comfort. You show emotional honesty among your peers. You ask for help when you need it. You take responsibility when you are wrong, without excuse.

People are watching. Your example gives others permission to be better.

lessons.title: Becoming an Advocate
lessons.content:
Advocacy means speaking up for change — in your family, community, school, or workplace.

You don't need a microphone or a platform to be an advocate. Advocacy starts in small moments: Having honest conversations with your brothers, friends, and sons about GBV. Sharing accurate information on social media. Challenging leaders respectfully when they say harmful things. Mentoring younger men and boys in your community.

Every advocate was once a bystander who decided to act. This is your moment.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: Where does a man's influence show up most powerfully?
options: A) Only in political or religious leadership positions
B) In everyday moments — jokes, comments, social media, how he treats women
C) Only when he has a large audience
D) Only in formal speeches
quiz.feedback: Correct. Influence is exercised in ordinary moments — what you laugh at, what you share, how you speak. These shape the people around you daily.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: Leading by example means:
options: A) Telling others what to do
B) Consistently behaving in ways that align with the values you claim to hold
C) Being perfect at all times
D) Only acting when others are watching
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. Real leadership is consistency between your private behaviour and your public values — not performance.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: Advocacy in ending GBV can look like:
options: A) Only organised marches and protests
B) Sharing honest conversations, calling out harmful speech, mentoring younger men
C) Letting organisations handle it
D) Only speaking up if you have a large social media following
quiz.feedback: Correct. Advocacy is everyday action — conversations, challenges, mentorship. You don't need a platform. You need courage.

modules.title: Community Action & Advocacy
modules.opening_story:
Meet Segun.

Segun is 27. He lives in Ibadan. After completing a GBV training, he went back to his community and started a conversation — just him and five friends under a mango tree.

He shared what he had learned. He asked questions. He listened.

Within a month, the group grew to 30 men. They called themselves the "Ibadan Brothers' Circle."

They started holding weekly meetings. They began sharing information in WhatsApp groups. They organised a community dialogue.

One of their members stopped his friend from beating his wife. Another reported a case of child marriage to the authorities.

Segun didn't have money. He didn't have a title. He had knowledge, commitment, and community. That was enough.

lessons.title: Why Community Action Matters
lessons.content:
Laws can be passed. Campaigns can be launched. But lasting change happens community by community, relationship by relationship.

Communities are where norms live. They are where children learn what is normal. They are where survivors are believed — or silenced.

When communities change, everything changes: Survivors are more likely to speak out. Abusers are less protected by silence. Young people grow up with healthier models. Women's rights become community values, not just legal ones.

You are a part of a community. And communities are changed by their members.

lessons.title: The Power of Storytelling
lessons.content:
Stories change minds faster than statistics. When people hear facts, they think. When they hear stories, they feel. And behaviour changes through feeling.

Sharing your own story — your journey of learning, questioning, and changing — gives other men permission to do the same.

Ways to use storytelling: Share your journey on social media. Speak at community meetings, youth groups, or religious gatherings. Write a short message and share it in your family or friend WhatsApp group. Talk one-on-one with a friend who needs to hear it.

lessons.title: How to Engage Your Community
lessons.content:
You don't need a budget or an NGO to engage your community. You need intention and consistency.

Practical community engagement: Start a men's conversation group — even three people is enough. Organise a community dialogue on GBV — in a church, mosque, community hall, or under a tree. Use WhatsApp groups to share helpful content. Partner with local organisations, schools, or religious bodies. Identify and work with existing community leaders — chiefs, pastors, imams.

Change is not a project. It is a practice. Start small. Stay consistent. Grow.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: Why is community action important in ending GBV?
options: A) Laws and campaigns alone are not enough — norms change community by community
B) Communities have no role — it is a government job
C) Only urban communities matter
D) Community action is too slow to make a difference
quiz.feedback: Correct. Norms are lived in communities. Laws protect rights — but communities determine what behaviour is acceptable. Both are needed.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: Why is storytelling powerful in advocacy?
options: A) Stories are more entertaining than facts
B) Stories make people feel, not just think — and behaviour changes through feeling
C) Stories are easier to make up
D) Stories only work for educated audiences
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. When people hear a real human story, they connect emotionally — and emotional connection is what changes minds and behaviour.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: What is needed to start a community men's group?
options: A) A large budget and NGO registration
B) A government permit
C) Intention, consistency, and even just 2-3 men to start
D) At least 50 members
quiz.feedback: Correct. Segun started with five friends under a mango tree. What matters is beginning — and staying consistent.

modules.title: Networks & Movement Building
modules.opening_story:
Meet Ibrahim, Emeka, Tunde, and Bello.

They all took different journeys. They come from different states, different tribes, different religions.

But they are now connected — through a WhatsApp group, through shared values, and through a commitment they made to themselves and each other.

Together, they have reached over 300 men in their communities. They share resources. They support each other when the work gets hard. They hold each other accountable.

None of them could have reached 300 men alone. But together, they are a movement.

When good men connect, the ripple goes further than anyone can see.

lessons.title: Why Networks Matter
lessons.content:
Individual effort is valuable. But networks multiply impact.

A network connects you with: Other men who share your values (reducing isolation). Resources, ideas, and strategies you might not have alone. Accountability — people who challenge and encourage you. Amplification — your message reaches further when others carry it too.

The Brothers' Room community group is your first network. Use it.

lessons.title: Collaboration Over Competition
lessons.content:
Many men in Nigeria are doing good work on GBV prevention. The work is too big for anyone to do alone — and too important to make it about themselves.

Collaboration means: Sharing information and resources across groups. Supporting other men's work, not competing with it. Reaching out to local organisations and offering your skills. Finding common ground across religious and ethnic differences.

Together we grow. Divided we go in circles.

lessons.title: Sustaining the Movement
lessons.content:
Movements die when people burn out or lose focus. Sustainability requires intention.

How to sustain your commitment: Keep your "why" close — revisit why you started. Celebrate small wins — change is slow; progress is worth celebrating. Rest — you cannot pour from an empty cup. Build systems, not just events — regular meetings, shared responsibilities. Bring in new voices — especially younger men. Document your impact.

The work is long. But it is worth it.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: Why do networks matter in social change work?
options: A) They make individuals look more important
B) They multiply impact, provide accountability and reduce isolation
C) They are mainly useful for fundraising
D) Only large networks matter
quiz.feedback: Correct. Networks amplify what individuals cannot do alone — they share resources, build resilience, and carry the message further.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: Collaboration over competition means:
options: A) Allowing only one organisation to lead all GBV work
B) Supporting other men's and organisations' work rather than competing with it
C) Only working with people from your own tribe or religion
D) Taking credit for all progress
quiz.feedback: Correct. The problem is too large for competition. Collaboration multiplies impact and builds a stronger, broader movement.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: To sustain a movement long-term, you should:
options: A) Work as hard as possible without stopping
B) Focus only on big events and campaigns
C) Build systems, celebrate wins, rest, and bring in new voices
D) Keep the core group small and exclusive
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. Sustainability requires systems, rest, and renewal — not just passion. Burn-out is the enemy of long-term change.

modules.title: Legal Frameworks & Human Rights
modules.opening_story:
Meet Kelechi.

Kelechi is 25, from Abuja. He has a neighbour, Obi, who regularly beats his wife, Chioma. One evening, after a loud fight, Kelechi tries to advise Obi. Obi snaps: 'Keep off! It is my house and my wife. The law has no business here.' Kelechi realizes many men believe the law stops at their front door. Today, we give him and you the truth about legal protections.

lessons.title: The VAPP Act in Nigeria
lessons.content: In reality, Nigeria passed the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act (VAPP Act) in 2015. This landmark law criminalizes domestic violence, rape, emotional abuse, and spousal abandonment. It is a federal crime, and marriage is never an excuse for violence. Legal frameworks exist to enter homes and hold abusers accountable.

lessons.title: Legal Rights & Protections
lessons.content:
The VAPP Act and other state laws provide strong protections for SGBV survivors. Under these laws, survivors have the right to seek protection orders (to keep abusers away), obtain medical and psychological support, and have their privacy protected in court.

Filing a report is free, and the state is responsible for prosecuting criminal acts. Understanding these rights is the first step to breaking the cycle of violence.

lessons.title: Reporting & Referral Channels
lessons.content:
If someone is experiencing abuse, knowing where to report can save a life. In Nigeria, key referral channels include:

1. NAPTIP (National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons) - handles violence against persons.
2. Family Support Units (FSUs) at designated police stations.
3. Human Rights Commissions and local NGOs providing legal aid and shelters.

As an ally, your role is to share these resources, support the survivor's choices, and help them contact authorities safely.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: Which of the following is TRUE under the VAPP Act in Nigeria?
options: A) Domestic violence is a private family matter
B) Spousal violence is a criminal offense and marriage is not an excuse
C) The police cannot interfere in marital disputes
D) Only physical violence is criminalized
quiz.feedback: Correct! The VAPP Act criminalizes spousal violence, and marriage is never a shield for abuse under Nigerian law.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: What right do SGBV survivors have under the VAPP Act?
options: A) The right to be blamed for provoking the abuse
B) The right to seek protection orders and get medical support
C) No rights until the court finishes the case
D) Only the right to pay the police to investigate
quiz.feedback: Correct! Survivors have the legal right to seek protection orders, obtain medical/psychological support, and have their privacy protected.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: Which agency in Nigeria is specifically tasked with handling violence against persons (such as SGBV)?
options: A) EFCC
B) NAPTIP
C) NIS
D) Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC)
quiz.feedback: Correct! NAPTIP (National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons) handles the enforcement of the VAPP Act.

modules.title: Personal Action Plan
modules.opening_story:
Meet Emeka — one last time.

Six weeks ago, Emeka was a man who felt something was wrong but didn't have the words.

Today, he is different.

He has had a conversation with his younger brother about gender norms. He called out a degrading joke in his friend group. He apologised to Adaeze for the times he shut down instead of communicating. He found out about the VAPP Act and shared it in his family WhatsApp group.

He is not perfect. He still slips. But he is aware now in ways he was not before.

And awareness — honest, committed awareness — is where everything begins.

This is not the end of the course. This is the beginning of the work.

lessons.title: What You Now Know
lessons.content:
Over the past six weeks, you have covered:

✅ The difference between sex and gender | ✅ How harmful norms are created and passed on | ✅ What SGBV is, its types, and its impact | ✅ The root causes of GBV — power, culture, economy | ✅ Your role as a man in ending GBV | ✅ What healthy relationships and consent look like | ✅ How to intervene as a bystander | ✅ How to use your influence and become an advocate | ✅ How to engage your community and build networks | ✅ The legal frameworks that protect survivors in Nigeria

This is not just information. This is responsibility.

lessons.title: Building Your Personal Action Plan
lessons.content:
An action plan turns intention into practice. Your plan has three parts:

1. DAILY ACTIONS — What will you do every day? Examples: Speak respectfully to every woman in your life. Call out one harmful norm when you hear it. Check in on a friend who may be struggling.

2. WEEKLY ACTIONS — What will you commit to each week? Examples: Have one honest conversation about GBV with a man in your life. Share one resource from this course. Attend the Brothers' Room community check-in.

3. LONG-TERM COMMITMENTS — What will you build over time? Examples: Start a men's group in your community. Mentor one younger man. Report any cases of abuse I become aware of through proper channels.

Write your plan. Share it. Keep it.

lessons.title: Accountability and the Pledge
lessons.content:
Commitment without accountability fades. Accountability keeps commitment alive.

Your accountability tools: Your accountability buddy (check in weekly). The Brothers' Room community group (share your progress). Your personal action plan (review every Sunday). The bot (it will remind you of your pledge weekly for the next month).

Your public pledge: "I, [your name], commit to [specific action]. I will do this because I believe [your reason]. I will be held accountable by [name of person or group]."

This pledge is yours. But it belongs to your community too. Post it in the group. Say it out loud. Mean it.

Welcome to the Brotherhood of Change Agents.

quiz.question: Question 1 of 3: A personal action plan should include:
options: A) Only one big goal
B) Daily, weekly, and long-term commitments
C) A list of other people who need to change
D) Only things you are already doing
quiz.feedback: Correct. A strong action plan works at all levels — small daily habits, consistent weekly practices, and ambitious long-term commitments. All three are needed.

quiz.question: Question 2 of 3: Why is public accountability important?
options: A) To show off to others
B) To keep commitment alive and create social support for your goals
C) Because private commitments never work
D) It is not important — private commitments are enough
quiz.feedback: Correct. Public pledges create social accountability — the knowledge that others are watching motivates consistency, and community support sustains long-term change.

quiz.question: Question 3 of 3: Completing this course means:
options: A) You are now perfect and done with learning
B) You have the information — now the work of applying it begins
C) You can teach others without continuing to learn yourself
D) Your responsibility ended with Module 12
quiz.feedback: Exactly right. The course is the beginning, not the destination. The real work happens in your daily choices, your relationships, and your community — starting now.
